7.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which nail is this?"
- "Slotted tube, cloverleaf section, no holes → **Küntscher**; thin solid rod with a hook → **Rush pin**; curved rod with an eye → **Ender**."
- "Two thin flexible titanium rods with a curved tip → **elastic nail** (TENS = titanium elastic nailing system; Nancy nail) for children."
- "Thick cannulated nail with locking holes at both ends → **interlocking nail** (femur, tibia, humerus); head screws too → **cephalomedullary** (ch 6)."

### The one feature that tells each apart
| Nail | Look for | Section | Reamed / locked | Main use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Küntscher** | straight slotted tube, hole for the extraction hook (Nagah) | cloverleaf | reamed, not locked (AO) | transverse isthmic femur (Handbook) |
| **V-nail** | slotted tube | V-shaped | not locked (Handbook) | three-point fixation, like Küntscher (Handbook) |
| **Rush pin** | solid rod, hook and bevel (Handbook) | round, solid | unreamed, not locked (Nagah) | thin, unlocked → needed a cast (AO) |
| **Ender** | curved solid rod, eye (slot) at the end (Handbook) | round, solid | unreamed, not locked (Handbook) | thin, unlocked → needed a cast (AO) |
| **Nancy / TENS** | thin titanium rods, curved tip, colour-coded (Nagah) | round, solid | unreamed, not locked (Handbook) | children's shafts (Rockwood) |
| **Interlocking** | locking holes at both ends (Rockwood) | tube, mostly cannulated | reamed or not, locked (AO) | adult femur, tibia, humerus |
| **Cephalomedullary** | screw or blade into the head | cannulated | locked → ch 6 (Handbook) | proximal femur |

- IM (intramedullary) nail = rod in the medullary canal → **load-sharing** internal splint (Nagah)
- Classified by path → **condylocephalic** (from the condyles up) · **centromedullary** (standard nails) · **cephalomedullary** (Gamma, recon) (Handbook)

| 1976 | transfixing locking screws → interlocking nails (Handbook) |

- Locking screws introduced by **Grosse and Kempf** → indications widened to proximal, distal, complex fractures (AO)

| Generation | Feature | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **First** | no locking screws | Küntscher, V-nail, Rush, Ender, Nancy (Handbook) |
| **Second** | standard locking screws | interlocking femoral / tibial nail, recon (Handbook) |
| **Third** | anatomical shape, multiplanar locking | Gamma, expert tibial nail (Handbook) |

7.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a nail work?"
- "It is an internal splint on the **mechanical axis**: short lever arm, **load-sharing**, relative stability → **callus** healing (AO; Handbook)."
- "Inserted closed, away from the fracture → periosteum spared; locking screws hold **length and rotation** (AO)."

### Load sharing and the lever arm
- Fracture ends in contact → the nail **shares** load with bone · only in very comminuted shafts it bears all load (Rockwood)
- Nails resist **bending** very well → they need locking screws against **torsion and compression** (Miller)
- Stability is relative → healing is **secondary**, by callus, not direct bone healing (Nagah)

- Nail versus plate: shorter lever arm, round section (Handbook)
- Load sharing in bending between nail and bone (Campbell)

### Nail vs plate — the examiner's table
| | Nail | Plate |
|---|---|---|
| Load | sharing (Nagah) | bearing (Handbook) |
| Stability · healing | relative · secondary (Nagah) | absolute or relative · primary or secondary (Nagah) |
| Incision · reduction | small · indirect (Nagah) | open or MIPO (minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis) · direct (Nagah) |
| Blood supply hit | **endosteal** (Nagah) | **periosteal** (Nagah) |
| Lever arm | short, on the axis → less bending (Handbook) | long → bends more (Handbook) |
| Cross-section | round → small stress riser (Handbook) | rectangular → stress riser (Handbook) |

- Tibia → nail has better union; plates win only near the joints, with less malunion (AO)
- Humerus → plate and nail unite alike; nailing has more complications, mainly shoulder (AO)

### Diameter — "the power of 4"
- Rigidity rises with **diameter⁴** → 1.5 × diameter = 5 × rigidity (Handbook)
- Nails have both **bending and torsional** stiffness; plates, screws and fixators only bending (Handbook)

PITFALL — power of 3 or power of 4?
- Handbook → rigidity ∝ diameter⁴ for nails, plates and external fixators alike
- Miller → nail stiffness ∝ radius³ in **bending**, radius⁴ in **torsion**
- Say → "**Thicker nail, much stiffer: about the fourth power, especially in torsion.**"

### Working length
- Locked nail → distance between the **innermost proximal and distal screws** (Handbook)
- Unlocked nail → the part of the nail **not supported by bone** (Nagah)
- Bending stiffness ∝ **1/L²**, torsional stiffness ∝ 1/L → bending suffers more (Handbook)
- Longer working length → more fracture motion → may delay union (Miller)

### Design choices
| Choice | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Slotted** (Küntscher, universal) | elastic, adapts to the canal; weak in torsion (AO) |
| **Unslotted** | torsional stiffness up → biggest advantage of closed section (Miller) |
| **Solid** | lower infection susceptibility, no dead space (AO) |
| **Cannulated** | passes over a guide wire → easier insertion (AO) |
| **Titanium** | low stiffness, high fatigue strength → thin unreamed nails (AO) |

- Unreamed solid titanium femoral nail → **9 mm** · locking screws **4.2 / 4.9 mm** (AO)
- Nail curvature differs a little from the femoral bow → friction fit; big mismatch → hard insertion, fracture, malreduction (Miller)

7.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "effects of reaming?"
- "Mechanically: wider canal, more contact → **bigger, stronger nail** (AO)."
- "Biologically: debris acts as **local autograft**, perfusion of soft tissues rises; cost → endosteal blood flow, **heat**, intramedullary pressure, **fat emboli** (AO)."
- "Reamed nailing heals better → gold standard for closed femoral and tibial shafts (AO)."

### Reamed vs unreamed
| | Reamed | Unreamed |
|---|---|---|
| Nail | larger, stronger (AO) | small, solid, locking mandatory (AO) |
| Endosteal supply | inner **50–80%** of cortex devascularised (Miller) | preserved (Miller) |
| Pressure in canal | **420–1,510 mm Hg** (Rockwood) | 40–70 mm Hg (Rockwood) |
| Femoral nonunion | **1.6%** (AO) | **7.5%** (AO) |
| Implant failure | fewer screw breaks (AO) | more, smaller nails (Miller) |

- Endosteal circulation recovers in **8–12 weeks**; periosteum feeds the cortex meanwhile (AO)
- Awl, wire, reamer or nail acts as a **piston** → marrow pushed into the veins (AO)
- Intravasation after tibial fractures **19%** vs femoral **78%** → systemic impact far lower in the tibia (AO)

PITFALL — "does reaming reduce fat embolism?"
- Handbook and Nagah → reaming "reduces the risk of fat embolism"
- AO, Rockwood, Miller → reaming raises pressure and emboli; unreamed nails embolise less; clinical difference unproved
- Say → "**Reaming increases emboli; gentle, gradual reaming with sharp reamers limits them.**"

### Reamed nail in femur and tibia (bank question)
- Femur → reamed nailing = **gold standard** for isolated shaft fractures; union **95%** (AO)
- Polytrauma, chest injury → resuscitate first; unstable patient → **damage control**: external fixator, nail within **5–7 days** (AO)
- Vallier → definitive femoral nailing when **lactate <4.0 mmol/L** and **pH >7.25** after resuscitation (AO)
- Fixator kept **>2 weeks** → pin holiday **2–3 days** in traction before nailing (AO)

- Tibia, closed → reamed nail = method of choice; open → reamed and unreamed equal (AO)
- SPRINT (Study to Prospectively Evaluate Reamed Intramedullary Nails in Patients with Tibial Fractures) → **1,319** adults → reamed nails, fewer screw breaks in closed fractures (AO)

### Reaming technique
- Sharp, deep-fluted reamers · **0.5 mm** steps · stop at cortical "**chatter**" (AO)
- Tourniquet while reaming the tibia → some avoid it for heat; a randomised trial found it acceptable (AO)

- **RIA** (reamer–irrigator–aspirator) → less heat and pressure; also harvests graft (AO)
- RIA graft harvest → inner cortex thinned **>2 mm** risks a **donor-site fracture** · blood loss can be considerable (AO)
- Prophylactic nailing of intact bone → **distal venting hole** essential; venting cuts pressure **50–90%** (AO)

### Static vs dynamic locking
| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Screws | round holes, **above and below** (Handbook) | one segment only, or the oval hole set dynamic (Handbook) |
| Does | holds length, stops compression (Handbook) | allows controlled compression (Handbook) |
| For | comminuted, spiral, metaphyseal (Handbook) | stable transverse, short oblique (Rockwood) |

- Handbook sheet: cannulated nails, locking modes, dynamisation (Handbook)
- Dynamic versus static locking of a femoral nail (Campbell)

PITFALL — how many locking screws?
- Handbook → one above and one below if **mid-shaft + non-spiral + non-comminuted**; else two and two
- AO → femur always **static, two at top and bottom**; distally ≥2 to stop toggling
- Say → "**Two proximal and two distal, statically locked; one each only in a stable mid-shaft transverse fracture.**"

- Lock **distally first**, then "backstroke" the nail to close the gap, then lock proximally (AO)
- Distal locking screws = **weakest part** · fatigue strength ∝ screw diameter (AO)

- Backstroke: distal locking first, then closing the gap (AO)

### Dynamisation
- Remove the **static screw from the round hole** → the oval-hole screw keeps alignment while the fracture impacts (AO)
- Best at **2–3 months**; in the femur rarely, mainly for transverse fractures (AO)
- Primary (at surgery) or secondary (later) → remove both screws on the side **away from** the fracture (Nagah)
- **Autodynamisation** = broken locking screws → may heal or herald nonunion (AO)

### Blocking (Poller) screws
- Screw beside the nail path → narrows a **wide metaphyseal canal** → nail forced central, construct stiffer (AO)
- Placed **perpendicular** to the direction in which the nail would otherwise drift (AO)
- Rule → in the **short fragment**, on the **concave side** of the deformity (AO; Harborview)
- Valgus → screw **lateral** to the nail near the fracture, or medial far from it (Rockwood)

- Poller screws beside the nail, distal femur and tibia (AO)
- Blocking screws sit on the concave side, both planes (Harborview)
- Femoral valgus corrected by a blocking screw, X-rays (Rockwood)
- Poller screw blocks the old nail path in revision (AO)

- Screw basics → ch 4 · uses → alignment, extra stability, steering past an old sclerotic nail path (AO)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Poller: short fragment, concave side — block the wrong path**

7.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "transverse femoral shaft fracture — what do you do?"
- "Resuscitate, assess open or closed; closed or Gustilo I–II within 24 hours → **closed reamed statically locked nail** (Nagah; AO)."
- "Plan length and diameter on the normal side, use the **entry point of that nail**, ream to chatter, lock distally freehand, check rotation (AO)."

### Recognise it
- Piriformis nail → **straight**, slight anterior bow, uniform 4.5 mm screws (Handbook)
- Trochanteric nail → **proximal lateral bend** → enters at the GT (greater trochanter) tip (AO)

### Indications · contraindications
| Use it | Avoid it |
|---|---|
| Diaphyseal, open, segmental, pathological (Nagah) | infection at entry site or canal (AO) |
| Comminuted, osteoporotic (Nagah) | polytrauma with lung injury, unresuscitated (AO) |
| Polytrauma → early mobilisation (Nagah) | very narrow or deformed canal (AO) |
| Nonunion, malunion revision (Nagah) | metaphyseal fracture, screws too weak (AO) |

- OI (osteogenesis imperfecta), rickets, osteoporotic bone with several CORAs (centres of rotation of angulation) → **one osteotomy at each CORA** so the nail can pass · translation osteotomies block the nail (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- **Atypical (bisphosphonate) femoral fracture** → reamed locked nail · healing slow → stop the drug or a drug "holiday" (AO)

### Entry points
| Entry | Fits | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Piriformis fossa** | straight nail, in line with canal (AO) | prevents varus, subtroch (AO) | AVN (avascular necrosis) in open physes; neck fracture (AO) |
| **GT tip** | nail with lateral bend (AO) | easier, quicker, less muscle damage (AO) | reamer drifts lateral → varus (AO) |
| **Lateral to GT** | helical nail, turns 90° (AO) | easiest insertion (AO) | design-specific |

- Wrong nail for the entry → **malreduction** or iatrogenic fracture (AO)
- Too anterior → huge forces, proximal femur bursts · too posterior → lost reduction (AO)
- Lateral view → piriformis wire in line with the posterior third of the femur (AO)
- Trochanteric start → **slightly anterior** on the lateral view (Harborview)

- Entry points: piriformis, GT tip, lateral to GT (AO)
- Piriformis wire collinear with canal; nail-specific entries (AO)
- Piriformis fossa start, AP and lateral fluoroscopy (Harborview)
- Trochanteric start, AP and lateral fluoroscopy (Harborview)

PITFALL — piriformis entry in a child
- Pediatric piriformis entry → threatens the posterosuperior retinacular vessels → femoral head AVN (Miller)
- Adolescent with open physes → **trochanteric or lateral entry** only (Miller)
- Say → "**Never piriformis in an open physis; GT tip or lateral entry.**"

### Measuring length and diameter (bank question)
- Templates are unreliable → long-bone X-ray magnification varies **10–20%** (AO)
- Length → ruler imaged over the **intact femur**, or nails in their box imaged over the opposite thigh (AO)
- Ruler parallel to the shaft, both bone ends centred in the beam → else wrong length (AO)
- Nagah → box ruler on the **normal leg**; diameter read at the **isthmus** from its squares

- Diameter → special ruler, or the **reamer head as a probe** (AO)
- Antegrade nail ends at **mid-patella** level · retrograde → 7.5 (AO)

- Measuring nail length with C-arm and ruler (AO)

### Insertion — instruments in order
1) Antibiotic within the hour before incision; supine or lateral, traction table or free leg (Nagah; AO)
2) Stab incision proximal to the GT, in line with the canal (AO)
3) Awl or **3.0 mm cannulated drill** through a sleeve at the entry, checked AP (anteroposterior) and lateral (AO)
4) **Ball-tipped guide wire** across the reduced fracture to the distal physeal scar (Campbell)
5) Ream in **0.5 mm** steps to chatter → **1–1.5 mm** over the nail (Campbell)
6) Measure → insert the nail by hand, gentle taps; resistance → ream **0.5 mm** more (Campbell)
7) Distal screws **freehand** · proximal screws through the jig on the handle (AO)
8) Check length, alignment, rotation before proximal locking (AO)

- Nagah → two guide wires: **olive (ball-tipped)** so a reamer head cannot be lost, and a plain one
- Temporary **Schanz screws** for reduction → **monocortical in the proximal fragment** so they do not block the nail · bicortical distally (AO)
- Long oblique or subtrochanteric fracture the nail does not reduce → **one or two percutaneous cerclage wires** are safe if bone is not devitalised · leave them in (AO)

- Bead-tipped guide wire centred at the distal femur (Campbell)

### Freehand distal locking — "perfect circles"
1) C-arm lateral until the hole is a **perfect circle**; oval = wrong beam (Campbell)
2) Stab incision over the hole · drill tip on the circle at **45°** (Campbell)
3) Swing the drill **in line with the beam** → drill the near cortex (Campbell)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "elastic nails"
- "**TENS** (titanium elastic nailing system), or ESIN (elastic stable intramedullary nailing): two pre-bent flexible nails, **opposite curves**, each with **three-point fixation** (Campbell)."
- "Stable shaft fractures in children about **5–11 years**; avoids both physes (Miller; Campbell)."

### Recognise it
- Thin colour-coded titanium rods, curved tip · Nancy = the French city where it began (Nagah)
- Elastic nails per Ligier → implant of choice for children's long bones (Rockwood)

### How it works — three conditions
- Each nail bends → touches the canal at **three points** → rotational control (Handbook)
- Diameter → one nail **60%** of the canal · two nails **80%** together (Handbook)
- Apex of the curve **at the fracture** · curve height **3 ×** canal width (Handbook)
- Alternative for rigid unlocked nails → **bundle nailing** packs the canal (Handbook)

- Rotational control: bundle nailing and three-point fixation (Handbook)
- Two C-shaped, S plus C, and straight constructs (Campbell)

### Insertion (femur, retrograde)
1) Traction table → closed reduction under fluoroscopy (Campbell)
2) Nails sized to fill **≈80%** of the canal · bend them so the spread is widest at the fracture (Campbell)
3) Medial and lateral entry holes **≈2 cm** above the distal physis (Campbell)
4) Pass both to the fracture → reduce → advance into the proximal metaphysis, **not across the physis** (Campbell)
5) Leave the ends slightly proud for removal, not so long they block the knee (Campbell)

- Two divergent nails → retrograde elastic fixation is **stiffer in torsion than antegrade** in comminuted and transverse models (Campbell)

- Flexible nailing steps, femur, X-rays (Campbell)
- Femoral shaft fracture before and after elastic nails (Campbell)

### Limits
- Poorer results **>11 years** and in heavy or obese children (Miller)
- Complications fell **52% → 23%** when limited to stable fractures (Campbell)
- Older adolescents **12–16 years** → rigid trochanteric-entry nail instead of elastic nails (Campbell)
- Clavicle → elastic nails **2.0–3.0 mm**, medial to lateral (AO)

PITFALL — weight limit for elastic nails
- Campbell → use stainless-steel elastic nails, not titanium, in children above **49 kg**
- Miller → contraindicated above **100 lb** (≈45 kg), especially spiral patterns
- Say → "**About 45–50 kg is the ceiling; heavier or unstable → plate or rigid nail.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Two nails, 80% fill, apex at the fracture, curve three times the canal, stop short of the physis**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "complications of nailing?"
- "Most serious → **fat embolism** (Nagah); key technical error → **malalignment** from a wrong entry point (AO)."
- "Then nonunion, screw or nail breakage, infection, hip or knee pain at the entry (AO; Rockwood)."

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Malalignment** | wrong entry, wide metaphysis (AO) | correct entry, blocking screws (AO) |
| **Malrotation** | multifragmentary, no landmarks (AO) | LT shape sign, compare sides (AO) |
| **Nonunion** | instability, gap, infection (AO) | exchange nail or augment plate (AO) |
| **Screw or nail breakage** | fatigue before union (AO) | larger screws, all locking options (AO) |
| **Hip or knee pain** | antegrade or retrograde entry (AO) | warn the patient; remove if symptomatic (Rockwood) |
| **Wrong size** | short → stress riser at the tip · long → impingement (Nagah) | plan on the normal side (AO) |

### Fat embolism
- FES (fat embolism syndrome) → dyspnoea, confusion, petechiae · mortality **10–20%** (Handbook)
- Prevent → early stabilisation, careful reaming, damage control in bilateral femurs (Handbook)
- Order in multiple closed fractures → **femur, tibia**, pelvis or spine, upper limb (AO)

### Nonunion → exchange nailing
- Hypertrophic femoral nonunion → reamed nail, **larger diameter**, static locking (AO)
- Exchange nail at least **2 mm** larger than the index nail; ream 1 mm over it (Campbell)
- Alternative → leave the nail, add a **lateral augmentation plate** ± graft (AO)
- Miller → femur: plate and graft beat exchange · tibia: reamed exchange preferred, infection excluded first

- Exchange nailing of a femoral nonunion, X-rays (Campbell)
- Tibial nonunion united after exchange nailing (Campbell)

PITFALL — dynamise or exchange?
- AO → dynamise at **2–3 months** in suitable patterns; exchange for established nonunion
- Miller → dynamisation is less successful than exchange nailing for delayed union
- Say → "**Axially stable delayed union → dynamise; established or unstable → exchange a bigger reamed nail.**"

### Implant failure and the entry site
- Bent nail after new trauma → remove and replace; never straighten in situ (Campbell)
- HO (heterotopic ossification) at the entry **9–60%**, clinically significant **5–10%** (Rockwood)
- Hip pain after antegrade nailing **10–40%** → remove the nail only if symptomatic (Rockwood)
- Reamed antegrade nails → heterotopic bone **36%** vs **9%** unreamed (Rockwood)

- Bent femoral nail after repeated trauma (Campbell)
- Heterotopic ossification at the nail entry site (Rockwood)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line

7.09.1.b:
- FES (fat embolism syndrome) → dyspnoea, confusion, petechiae · mortality **10–20%** (Handbook)
- Prevent → early stabilisation, careful reaming, damage control in bilateral femurs (Handbook)
- Order in multiple closed fractures → **femur, tibia**, pelvis or spine, upper limb (AO)

7.09.2.b:
- Hypertrophic femoral nonunion → reamed nail, **larger diameter**, static locking (AO)
- Exchange nail at least **2 mm** larger than the index nail; ream 1 mm over it (Campbell)
- Alternative → leave the nail, add a **lateral augmentation plate** ± graft (AO)
- Miller → femur: plate and graft beat exchange · tibia: reamed exchange preferred, infection excluded first

- Exchange nailing of a femoral nonunion, X-rays (Campbell)
- Tibial nonunion united after exchange nailing (Campbell)

PITFALL — dynamise or exchange?
- AO → dynamise at **2–3 months** in suitable patterns; exchange for established nonunion
- Miller → dynamisation is less successful than exchange nailing for delayed union
- Say → "**Axially stable delayed union → dynamise; established or unstable → exchange a bigger reamed nail.**"

7.09.3.t: Implant failure and the entry site
7.09.3.b:
- Bent nail after new trauma → remove and replace; never straighten in situ (Campbell)
- HO (heterotopic ossification) at the entry **9–60%**, clinically significant **5–10%** (Rockwood)
- Hip pain after antegrade nailing **10–40%** → remove the nail only if symptomatic (Rockwood)
- Reamed antegrade nails → heterotopic bone **36%** vs **9%** unreamed (Rockwood)

- Bent femoral nail after repeated trauma (Campbell)
- Heterotopic ossification at the nail entry site (Rockwood)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Wrong entry → wrong axis · loose fit → Poller · no union → bigger nail**

7.10.b:
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What is this nail? | read the section and holes: clover, hook, eye, titanium pair, holes |
| Generations? | no locking · locking · anatomical multiplanar locking |
| Nail vs plate? | load-sharing, short lever arm, round section; endosteal vs periosteal hit |
| Power of 4? | rigidity ∝ diameter⁴; 1.5 × diameter = 5 × rigidity |
| Working length? | between innermost proximal and distal screws |
| Effects of reaming? | bigger, stronger nail, local autograft; cost endosteal blood flow, heat, fat emboli |
| Does reaming reduce fat embolism? | no → reaming increases emboli; gentle reaming with sharp reamers limits them |
| Reamed nail femur and tibia? | femur gold standard; closed tibia method of choice; open tibia equal |
| Static vs dynamic? | static holds length, stops compression; dynamic allows controlled compression |
| How many locking screws? | two and two, static; one each only if stable mid-shaft |
| Dynamisation? | remove the static screw from the round hole; best at 2–3 months |
| Blocking screws? | short fragment, concave side; narrows a wide metaphyseal canal |
| Transverse femoral shaft — steps? | resuscitate, plan, entry, ream to chatter, nail, lock distally, check |
| Measure length and diameter? | ruler over the intact femur; diameter at the isthmus or reamer head |
| Piriformis vs trochanteric entry? | straight nail vs lateral bend; never piriformis in an open physis |
| Freehand distal locking? | perfect circle, drill tip at 45°, then in line with the beam |
| PFN entry? | GT tip or just medial, per design → ch 6 |
| Retrograde nail: when? | obesity, floating knee, neck or acetabulum, bilateral, pregnancy |
| Tibial entry? | medial edge of the lateral tibial spine, anterior to the joint |
| Proximal-third tibia deformity? | valgus and procurvatum → semi-extend, Poller |
| Humeral nail entry? | sulcus medial to the greater tuberosity, through the cuff |
| Elastic nails? | two nails, 80% fill, three-point fixation, 5–11 years |
| Rush, Ender, Nancy? | Rush solid rod, hook · Ender curved rod, eye · Nancy titanium elastic |
| Complications of nailing? | fat embolism, malalignment, nonunion, breakage, entry pain |
| Nonunion after nailing? | exclude infection; exchange ≥2 mm larger or augment plate |
